book.title: Feel the Fear and Do It Anyway
book.author: Susan Jeffers

confidence_note: The reference TR text says Jeffers researched clients' fear of saying no and found that people who could say no gave a more valuable yes. That framing cannot be confirmed as a finding of the book and is not presented as one. The book does address people-pleasing, taking responsibility for your own life instead of blaming others, and, notably, the language of powerlessness. Jeffers suggests replacing 'pain' words with 'power' words: 'I can't' becomes 'I won't', 'I should' becomes 'I could', 'It's not my fault' becomes 'I'm totally responsible', 'It's a problem' becomes 'It's an opportunity', 'Life's a struggle' becomes 'Life's an adventure'. The story builds on the 'I can't' to 'I won't' shift as it applies to saying no.
facts: Jeffers argues that the words we use shape how powerful or powerless we feel.
She contrasts a vocabulary of pain with a vocabulary of power.

Examples she gives: replace 'I can't' with 'I won't'; replace 'I should' with 'I could'; replace 'It's not my fault' with 'I'm totally responsible'; replace 'It's a problem' with 'It's an opportunity'; replace 'Life's a struggle' with 'Life's an adventure'.
'I can't' presents you as a victim of circumstances; 'I won't' presents you as making a choice.
'I should' carries guilt and pressure; 'I could' opens options.
She argues that taking responsibility for your choices, rather than blaming others, is the foundation of moving past fear.
tension: People who can't say no often explain it as 'I couldn't refuse.' Jeffers asks whether that's true.
opening_idea: Listen to the words people use when they agree to things they don't want: 'I can't say no.'
reflect: Where do you say 'I can't' when you mean 'I won't'?
Which 'should' in your life is really a 'could'?
reflect_final: What request could you answer this week with an honest 'I won't'?

use_cases.situation: A colleague asks you to take on extra work you don't have time for.
use_cases.move: Say 'I won't be able to take this on this week' as a clear choice, not an excuse.

use_cases.situation: You feel guilty about all the things you 'should' do on the weekend.
use_cases.move: Rewrite the list as 'I could' and choose two.

use_cases.situation: A relative keeps pressing you to attend every family event.
use_cases.move: Answer kindly but clearly: 'I won't make it this time, but I'll come next month.'

pocket_idea: Say 'I won't' instead of 'I can't,' and you'll notice who's choosing.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: 'I can't' makes you a victim; 'I won't' makes you the one choosing.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Pain vs power vocabulary: can't/won't, should/could, problem/opportunity.
conversation_variants.question_idea: Where do you say 'I can't' when you mean 'I won't'?
